# Major Event Reviews

US & Europe: Severe Convective Storm

US SCS YTD: Economic losses reached USD61 billion

as the portion covered by insurance is now up to

USD46 billion

US: Insured SCS losses already amount to the fourth-costliest year on record: only behind 2023, 2024, and 2020

US: At least 17 individual billion-dollar economic loss outbreaks; 13+ also resulted in a billion-dollar (or more) insured loss

Europe: Generally benign

SCS season compared to recent years; costliest stretch occurred in France during May and June

United States

SCS losses in the US continued to drive a substantial portion of global insured SCS losses during the first nine months of

2025. Most of the losses were incurred following a highly active period for the peril during the peak months between March and June. US SCS accounted for 44% of global insured losses alone through Q3. To date, the US has experienced 13 billion-dollar insured SCS loss events, of which five saw multi-billion-dollar industry loss totals (USD2+ billion).

2025 marked the third consecutive year in which US SCS insured losses through September exceeded USD40 billion. When extending to the full calendar year, 2025 already ranks as the fourth-costliest year for insurers on record - only behind 2023 (USD62 billien), 2024 (USD57 billien), and 2020 (USD47 billion).

As some of the larger 2025 outbreaks continue to be assessed and claims are processed, further loss progression is expected in the months ahead.

A persistent characteristic of 2025 SCS outbreaks has been instances of torrential rainfall spawning flash flooding. These SCS driven flash-flooding events were aided by multiple factors, which included cut-off (stuck) low pressure systems in tandem with persistent flow from the Gulf and / or training (repeating) storms that formed near urban regions or recent burn scars. Notable events included flash flooding in the Texas Hill Country, Ruidoso (New Mexico), New York City (New York), Chicago (lilinois, and Milwaukee (Wisconsin) among others. In many instances, low National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) take up rates meant most of the flood-related damage went uninsured.
